utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We continue final submissions today. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence is presenting its closing oral arguments today. With a few prior comments, I wish to inform the Court about the way in which the Defence will present its closing arguments. Firstly, the Defence, believing that it would be of assistance to the Court, will present the evidence within the appropriate legal context. It will also indicate what are the requirements of international law with regards to important aspects of the doctrine of responsibility of a superior officer and/or superior, and bring it into correlation with the evidence presented within this case. This part of the closing arguments will be presented by my learned colleague Guenael Mettraux. In the second part, I will speak briefly about some positions presented in the closing arguments of the Prosecutor and other issues raised in the closing briefs, in final briefs of the Prosecutor. The Defence will not repeat the arguments already presented in the final brief, Your Honours. Your Honours, in order to assist the Chamber and our colleagues to follow our presentation, but also to use time economically, we have prepared documents that the Defence will use within the presentation and also a list of evidence, exhibits, and references that will be used. I will also make a few comments during the process. Defence has submitted several requests for transcript verification, and I need to say with gratitude that CLSS followed our requests. In numerous cases, it has submitted to the Court corrigenda to the transcript, and we also received some of the answers in the recent days. The Defence noticed that the Prosecution has cited to uncorrected transcripts, and some of the mistakes made are based on that usage of uncorrected transcripts. I believe that you will have, Your Honours, all corrected transcripts from this trial. The issue of translation has been one of the issues frequently raised within this process. Numerous issues have been resolved. The meaning of some of the notions has been clarified through the witnesses before this Court; however, Your Honours, you will still find different translations of the same notion in various documents. It was not possible to remove all such cases. We believe that it would not be of such significant to have an impact on the just verdict, and now I give the floor to my colleague, Guenael Mettraux. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning Mr. President. And perhaps before we start, and with the assistance of the usher, we will distribute the binders in question. Your Honours, the Prosecution case against Mr. Boskoski is that at the time of the alleged crimes, as a minister of the interior, he was de jure and de facto the superior of the alleged perpetrators and that, in that capacity and having effective control over the perpetrators, he was required to investigate their actions and failed to do so. In support of its contention that Mr. Boskoski was de jure and de facto the superior of those alleged to have committed the crimes, the Prosecution has referred to a number of decisions rendered by Mr. Boskoski in 2001, and cites from a number of provision from the Macedonian law. The evidence that the Prosecution has put forward in support of this part of its case proves only two things: First, that in 2001, Mr. Boskoski was the minister of the interior of the Republic of Macedonia; secondly, that all through 2001, he, in fact, exercised the powers given to him by law in Macedonia. These two facts, Your Honour, were never in dispute. Beyond this, however, the Prosecution has failed to prove any of the elements that would allow this Chamber to make a finding of superior responsibility vis-a-vis Mr. Boskoski. In particular, the evidence does not establish any sort of relationship of subordination between Mr. Boskoski and the alleged perpetrators. Such a relationship of subordination and not the fact of Mr. Boskoski's ministership was the fact which the Prosecution was required to prove at trial. As a separate requirement of effective control, the Prosecution asserts its success in establishing that element but did not provide a basis that would allow a reasonable trier of fact to agree with that assertion. As a preliminary matter, Your Honour, the Defence would note, once again, that the Prosecution has failed to identify a single alleged perpetrators of the crimes charges and failed to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that any of them was a de jure member of the MOI at the time. The Defence does not hereby suggest that the Prosecution would be required to identify the perpetrators by name. However, and as a minimum, the Prosecution would be required to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the perpetrators were part of an identifiable group of subordinates which was under the control of the superior at the relevant time. In this particular case, there is no basis to conclude that Mr. Boskoski had any authority or control, effective or otherwise, over a group of men which had been set up on an ad hoc basis with a view to carry out an operation that was decided and ordered by the president of the Republic of Macedonia. The fact that these men were variously referred to as members of the security forces or police reservists cannot make up for the fact that none of them was actually and effectively shown to have been a de jure member of the ministry at the time. The principle question which this Chamber has to decide, and that which the Prosecution has carefully avoided yesterday in its submission, is not whether a volunteer could become a police reservists without all the legal requirements being met, but whether those men who entered Ljuboten on the 12th of August of 2001 had become members of the reserve at the time. This fact has not been proved. Under the Appeals Chamber's jurisprudence, Your Honours, Mr. Boskoski's alleged ability to control the perpetrators would have to be established at the time when the crimes are said to have been committed. Accordingly, the Prosecution reference, for instance, to Minister Boskoski's decisions of employment or redeployment is not evidentially indicative of any degree of effective control on his part over the perpetrator and is, in fact, irrelative to the charges since it is temporarily unrelated to those events and demonstrate no sort of authority over those concerned by the requirement of effective control; namely, the perpetrators. This is why, for instance, the Trial Chamber in Ntagurera, at paragraph 637, rejected an argument by the Prosecution similar in kind to the one now being made in this courtroom. The Chamber said this: "While there is ample evidence that Bagambiki requisitioned gendarmes to provide security at a number of sites, there is insufficient evidence that he maintained any control over how these gendarmes carried out their mission upon deployment." The finding was upheld on appeal and the same reasoning would lead this Trial Chamber to conclude to the irrelevance of decisions of redeployment or employment which the Prosecution has put forth. Equally irrelevant, Your Honour, are decisions of mobilisation and demobilisation of reservists, which Mr. Boskoski adopted as minister. Those do not pertain to any sort of control over the alleged perpetrators during those events, nor do they demonstrate any authority to punish on the part of Mr. Boskoski. In Ntagurera again, the Trial Chamber, paragraph 636, rejected, again, the same argument that the Prosecution is now putting forward in this case. The Chamber said this: "After reviewing the relevant provisions of Rwandan law, the Chamber is not convinced that Bagambiki's ability to requisition gendarmes gave him de jure authority to give orders to them during the execution of an operation." Again, that finding wag upheld on appeal; and, again, the same reasoning and the same finding would have to be made by this Chamber. Let us now to turn to consider more closely, Your Honour, the evidence which the Prosecution has put forward in support of its case that Mr. Boskoski had superior authority and effective control over those who allegedly committed crimes in the village of Ljuboten on 12th August. It is the Prosecution case and the only case validly pleaded in the indictment that Mr. Boskoski at the time was able to exercise effective control over Mr. Tarculovski, who, in turn, would have been able to exercise some sort of authority over the alleged perpetrators. The Prosecution has failed to establish either aspects of that factual proposition. The Prosecution first relies upon the evidence given by M-052 to the effect that three to five weeks before those events, someone pretending to be Minister Boskoski called to say that someone would come to his station and that, the next day or so, Mr. Tarculovski allegedly claiming to have come on the authority of the minister arrived. Your Honours, there is simply no valid basis to regard this evidence as true or reliable. There is no evidence to corroborate the allegation that such a phone call ever took place, and the Defence has explained in its brief why M-052 is a intrinsically unreliable witness for whom, as a minimum, corroboration is necessary. It is telling in that regard that the telephone records of M-052 do not support this story, and the Prosecution was unable to prove the existence of such a call based on all the phone records that they reviewed. M-052 did not record this alleged incident in any Official Note or any record that he kept at the time. (redacted), he had claimed that such a conversation had taken place on 10 or 11 August, 2001; but no doubt when he was later made aware that there existed telephone records which would have shown his evidence to be false, he moved that alleged phone calls to the month of July, beyond those records. The implied suggestion contained in the Prosecution's final brief at paragraph 288, that M-053 somehow corroborated M-052's story on that point, is plainly wrong. Although M-053 indicated that he had seen Mr. Tarculovski on two occasions prior to the 11th of August, he made it clear at trial that it was in the month of August of 2001, and the record suggest that it would have been on the 10th. Never did M-053 suggest having heard of a call from Minister Boskoski to M-052. Even if such a call had taken place, there is no reliable evidence, Your Honour, that it was, in fact, Mr. Boskoski who was on the other side of the line. M-052 never claimed that he had been able to ascertain or verify that fact. Furthermore, there is no evidence that such a call was in any way related to the events of Ljuboten, and the Prosecution never put that suggestion to M-052 himself. The Defence submits that this uncorroborated story should be disregarded as unreliable. The Prosecution also seeks to rely upon another part of M-052's evidence; namely, the suggestion that at some point prior to the action, Mr. Tarculovski called Mr. Boskoski to agree to the use of a Hermeline vehicle. Again, Your Honour, there is no reliable basis that would permit a reasonable trier of fact to regard this evidence as true or reliable. The telephone records said by the Prosecution to have been used by Mr. Tarculovski during that weekend do not reveal any call from that phone to any of the phones used by Mr. Boskoski. Mr. Tarculovski never claimed that such a call took place, whether before the second commission or anywhere else. (redacted) (redacted) and never recorded in any official record, note, or otherwise. Even if M-052 had been truthful about what was allegedly told to him by Mr. Tarculovski, there is no evidence that Mr. Tarculovski actually made any contact with Mr. Boskoski on that occasion, and M-052 does not claim that he would have been in a position to verify this. The evidence is clear, Your Honour, that it (redacted) (redacted). It is equally apparent from the record and consistent with M-052's pattern of false stories that this story of a phone call between Mr. Tarculovski and Mr. Boskoski in -- is no more than another attempt to try to place on to others the responsibility for his own actions. The Prosecution next relies upon a third piece of the evidence of M-052, again uncorroborated. One where he claims that Zoran Krstevski was present in Cair on 10 August 2001, and that at the time Mr. Krstevski was or might have been an advisor to Ljube Boskoski. There is no corroboration for the evidence of M-052 that Zoran Krstevski was in the area at the time, and this evidence should be regarded for that reason already. M-052 did not record the alleged presence of Mr. Krstevski in any document, Official Note, or otherwise. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No other witness claims to have seen Mr. Krstevski in the area at the time, and this allegation was not put by the Prosecution to any of the witnesses who might have been capable of giving evidence on that point, in particular M-053. The evidence cited by the Prosecution in footnote 846 of its final brief, which it claims sports the evidence of M-052 on that point, does not, in fact, corroborate it to any relevant extent. The Defence simply invites, Your Honour, to look at tab 2 and 3 in your binder to ascertain that point for yourself. Even if it were accepted that Zoran Krstevski had gone to the area on the 10th of August, there is no evidence in what capacity he would have been there, whether as a journalist or otherwise. The evidence shows that, at the time, he did not work for Mr. Boskoski or for the Ministry of Interior. Exhibit P574, to the extent that it might suggest otherwise, has been shown to be unreliable, and it is contrary to the uncontested evidence that Mr. Krstevski, in fact, only left his job as a TV journalist and joined the MOI in September of 2001. I invite Your Honours to look at tab 4, 4A, 5, and 5A of the binder. Furthermore, the evidence of M-052 on that point does not provide any support for the Prosecution's effective control case, as there is no evidence of Mr. Krstevski having played any part in that operation or being present in the area at the time of the action. The Prosecution next appear to rely upon the presence of, it says, both Mr. Tarculovski and Mr. Boskoski in the yard of Brace's house to suggest that they met at the time. There is, in fact, no evidence that the two of them met or even saw each other on the 12th of August, 2001; nor is there any evidence, as the Prosecution has alleged in its brief, that the two of them were in Brace's yard at the same time. The evidence cited by the Prosecution in support of that proposition does not support such a finding. We invite the Chamber to look at tab 6 and 7 of your binder. There is, in fact, no evidence that Mr. Boskoski saw or recognised Mr. Tarculovski on that day. There is no evidence that Mr. Boskoski knew that he was there. No evidence that Mr. Boskoski had any contact with Mr. Tarculovski in relation to that action. No evidence that Mr. Boskoski would have had any means to control Mr. Tarculovski at that time, or that he had any reason to think that he should or could. Instead of supporting a case that Mr. Boskoski had any control over Mr. Tarculovski at the time, the evidence plainly shows that he had no means, no authority, and no reason to control him. Mr. Tarculovski was sent to the area at the behest and with an order of the president of the Republic, a fact that the Prosecution appears to be oblivious to. The record suggests that Mr. Tarculovski and the president were in regular phone contact during that weekend and that, while he was in the area, Mr. Tarculovski was exercising the authority of the president and executing the mandate that he had been given by him. When introducing himself to others, Mr. Tarculovski would introduce himself as a member of the security arrangement of the president, not as a police officer. Those with whom he dealt during that weekend understood that he was there as the man of the president. As mentioned by Mr. Krstevski, whilst he was in the area, Mr. Tarculovski was executing not any MOI-related task but implementing the will and the authority of the president. There is no disputes that at the time Mr. Tarculovski was an employee of the MOI. As such, he and Mr. Boskoski were connected from an institutional point of view, but that institutional relationship has been shown to be devoid of any value as far as would be relevant to establishing a relationship of effective control between the two of them. The combined evidence of Mr. Krstevski, Trajkovski, and Jakovoski proved beyond any doubt that the president was the sole master of the security arrangement of his security arrangement and that of his family, and that the MOI hierarchy exercised no control or influence over members and the activities of that sector. At paragraph 287 of its final brief, the Prosecution makes the strange assertion that witness Zoran Trajkovski was the chief of security of the MOI and, thus, a superior of Mr. Tarculovski. Clearly, that is wrong and misunderstands or misinterprets the evidence of Mr. Trajkovski and Keskovski about the structure of the security sector of the MOI. Mr. Trajkovski was not in a relationship of superior authority vis-a-vis Mr. Tarculovski, de jure or otherwise, nor was such a proposition put to him by the Prosecution at trial. Although the Prosecution did not allege that Mr. Boskoski would have been able to exercise effective control directly over the alleged perpetrators of crimes or that he could have used any other conduit than Mr. Tarculovski, the Defence should point out that the evidence would in any case not support such a proposition. The evidence is clear that as he arrived in Ljubanci, Mr. Boskoski had had no idea about the very existence of an operation; therefore, he had had no opportunity and no proven ability and authority to give any order in relation to that operation as might have been relevant to the charges. Outside of Mr. Boskoski's alleged authority over Mr. Tarculovski, the only element to which the Prosecution points to in its final brief is the evidence of Mr. Jakovoski that when Mr. Boskoski entered the yard at Brace's house, it was his impression that some people who were present stood at attention. First, it should be noted that Mr. Jakovoski, himself, made it clear that what he understood by that was that those in the courtyard stood still and greeted the minister. Whilst this evidence could at best demonstrate some degree of respect for the minister, it would not demonstrate any sort of control relevant to the doctrine of superior responsibility. The Tribunal has made it clear that the belief, even if held in good faith, or the appearance that the accused was a person of authority, does not dispense with the need to establish that he had actual authority and control over the perpetrators; nor is the fact that he may have influence, even substantial influence, over the perpetrator sufficient. At paragraph 306 of the Celebici appeals judgement, for instance, the Appeals Chamber said the following in relation to the accused Hazim Delic: "The fact that the detainees regarded him as the deputy commander and as a person with influence over the guards is not conclusive evidence of his actual authority." In other words, evidence that the accused held a position of authority and that this fact was acknowledged by others is no proof of effective control on his part. In Kordic, for instance, the Trial Chamber noted that Mr. Kordic was a politician with "tremendous influence and power," that he held an important position in the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, that he played an important military role, even at times issuing orders and exercising authorities over HVO forces, and that, in fact, he exercised "substantial influence." Despite having exercised such extensive authority, the Trial Chamber correctly found that Kordic could not be said to have been in effective control. In Celebici, the Trial Chamber noted, among other things, that Mr. Delalic's "general recognition and appreciation," paragraph 561, did not demonstrate effective control on his part. Whilst in Kvocka, the Chamber concluded that Mr. Kvocka did not have effective control, despite the fact that he had clear and broad authority and influence within the camp, that a former inmate said in evidence that he understood him to have been the commander of that camp, that guards made it clear that they could not allow certain things to within that camp without Mr. Kvocka's prior approval, that Mr. Kvocka, himself, addressed prisoners in the course of their detention and that he told them that he was in charge. Furthermore, even assuming that the people who greeted Minister Boskoski at Brace's house were reservists of the ministry rather than self-appointed volunteers, the Prosecution has failed to establish that any of those present in the courtyard at the time had taken any culpable part in any of the crimes charged in the indictment or that Mr. Boskoski would have been able to exercise any control over them at the time of the alleged crimes. Finally, it should be noted that the Prosecution has not pleaded and has not established that Mr. Boskoski -- I apologise, that Mr. Tarculovski had effective control over the alleged perpetrators. There is no evidence that he gave any orders to any of the alleged perpetrators, nor that any of them ever reported to him; nor is there any evidence, Your Honour, of a proven material ability on the part of Mr. Tarculovski to punish any of them for crimes that they allegedly committed. In those circumstances, the chain of effective control that allegedly linked Mr. Boskoski to the alleged perpetrators may be said to be broken not at one, but in two places in that chain. Let us turn to the other sites of alleged crime, Your Honour, the police stations, the court, and the hospital. It is quite remarkable, Your Honours, that the Prosecution final brief does not make any submissions as regards the alleged existence of a relationship of effective control between Mr. Boskoski and those said to have committed crimes in those locations. The Defence, therefore, invites the Trial Chamber to regard this part of the Prosecution case as having been effectively abandoned. In any case, the record is clear that at no point, whilst the alleged crimes were ongoing, did Mr. Boskoski learn of such events. He did not know of the presence of civilians in those locations, he did not know of any crimes being committed in those locations, and he had no proven ability to control any of the men said to have been involved in those events. The first unverified rumours that crimes might have been committed in some of those locations reached him in September of 2001, long after the time when he is said to have been able to exercise control over the perpetrators. In the absence of the necessary element of knowledge, and without any reason to act and no proven ability to do so, he could not possibly have exercised any sort of control over the perpetrators at the relevant time. This part of the case should fail for that reason also. In conclusion, Your Honours, the Defence submits that the Prosecution has failed to establish that Mr. Boskoski was in a relationship of superior/subordinate with the perpetrators and that he exercised effectively control over them at the time relevant to the charges, whether directly or through Mr. Tarculovski. It is our submission, Your Honours, that Mr. Boskoski should be acquitted for that reason alone. I would move on from the issue of control, Your Honour, to that of the steps which the Prosecution claims should have been taken by Mr. Boskoski. The Prosecution did not just go to the wrong door, Your Honours, as we had told you in our opening statement, but they went to the wrong house in the wrong neighbourhood. The entire Prosecution case is premised upon a grave misunderstanding of the way in which the Macedonian state has organised the way in which criminal investigations and disciplinary proceedings are carried out and which of its organs are competent in that matter. In this particular case, the Prosecution has sought to attribute to Mr. Boskoski duties and responsibilities that were never his own but those of the judiciary, or in some cases those of other organs within the ministry. The responsibility of a superior for the purpose of the doctrine of superior responsibility is not made of the accumulation of duties and responsibilities of his subordinates. This is also true of the duties and responsibilities of the minister of the interior of Macedonia. As was made clear in evidence, his duties and responsibilities are expressively and restrictively provided for in the relevant laws and by-laws. Identifying what were the duties and obligations of a superior under the relevant legal regime is critically important to determining, in turn, the scope of his potential responsibility as a superior, and here is why. After the First World War, Your Honour, the Commission on Responsibility of the Authors of War, the commission that had been set up by the five main Allied powers, noted the following as regard the responsibility of civilian leaders and military commanders: "To establish responsibility in such cases, it is elementary that the individual sought to be punished should have knowledge of the commission of the acts of a criminal nature and that he should have possessed the power, as well as the authority, to prevent, to put an end to, or repress them. Neither knowledge of the commission, nor ability to prevent, is alone sufficient. The duty or obligation to act is essential. They must exist in conjunction and a standard of liability which does not include them all is to be rejected." The point that the commission was making and which was later many times reiterated, Your Honours, is that superior responsibility, as a form of liability for a mission, may only be engaged where the superior has breached a duty which was binding on him to take a particular step or to adopt a particular measure. A number of Chambers of this Tribunal have noted that the requirement of a pre-existing duty to take steps or measures did not necessarily mean that the accused had to have the legal competence to adopt those. The Defence does not propose to address the correctness of that view in general terms and whether such a position is, in fact, supported under customary international law. The point that matters to present proceedings has been decided by the Appeals Chamber and our submissions would, therefore, be limited to this point: The Appeals Chamber has made it clear that in a case such as the present one, where the alleged basis for a duty to act is to be found in the law that regulates the role and position of the accused, it is that law which is determinative of the scope of the obligation which, if breached, could have the effect of engaging that superior's criminal responsibility. At paragraph 183 of the Halilovic appeals judgement, for instance, the Appeals Chamber made it clear that the applicable domestic laws and internal regulations of a particular state, in that case Bosnia and Herzegovina, effectively set "the framework of a commander's material ability to punish his subordinates." In other words, where the basis of an accused alleged authority lies in a position or role that is sanctioned and recognised by law, as in the case of Mr. Boskoski's ministership, the limits of what that superior would be required to do under the doctrine of superior responsibility would be set by the terms of that law. In the Halilovic case, the Trial and then the Appeals Chamber, therefore, carefully reviewed the law relevant to Mr. Halilovic's role as head of an inspection team to determine whether it included not just a material ability to do certain things but duties and obligations relevant to the effective prevention and pursuant of crimes. Duties and obligations. I draw your attention to paragraph 148 and 214 of the Halilovic appeals judgement, in particular. In the present case, Your Honours, the Prosecution has failed to establish that by law, Mr. Boskoski bore any of the duties which he said to have failed to fulfil. In other words, and even if one accepts for the sake of the argument that he did not do those things which the Prosecution he should have done, these were not his duties and obligation as understood by the Appeals Chamber, and a failure to adopt them would not be such as to entail his superior responsibility. There is another problem of compatibility of the Prosecution's theory with international law and domestic Macedonian law. International law makes it clear that where the basis of the alleged authority of the accused over the perpetrators lies in a position of authority that is recognised by law and regulated by law, the relevant domestic regime would be relevant not only to establishing the duties and obligations of a superior but also determine the nature of his mandate and function; the nature of his mandate and function, and, therefore, the outer reach of his liability. The findings made by the military Tribunal in the High Command case in relation to the accused von Leeb is a case in point. The Tribunal in this case emphasised the fact that, as commander in chief of an army group, the duties imposed upon von Leeb were exclusively operational, so that he had none of the executive powers that were said by the Prosecution to be relevant to the charges. The Tribunal went on to remark that his authority in the field of executive power was more in the nature of a right to intervene than a direct responsibility; page 554 and 555. The Tribunal find that, in those circumstances, it was not considered that criminal liability attached to him merely on the theory of subordination and overall command. I would indicate, in passing, that the Appeals Chamber in the Halilovic case adopted that jurisprudence wholeheartedly; paragraph 212 to 214. Therefore, where domestic law places upon different organ the responsibility of leading an investigation into allegations of crimes, or where the law has circumscribed the responsibility of the accused in such a way that he has no or limited duties in that regard, the accused could not, in principle, be held criminally responsible for failing to do so himself or for limiting his involvement to what the law demands of him. What may be concluded also from what has just been said, Your Honours, is that a superior officer or a state official could not be held criminally responsible pursuant to that doctrine in relation to measures that laid by reason of their nature outside the realm of his competencies. Turning again to the case of Mr. Boskoski, and taking on board the requirements of international law as just outlined, it can be concluded that Mr. Boskoski bore none of the duties and obligation which the Prosecution charges him with failing to adopt. Effectively, the Prosecution has charged Mr. Boskoski with what would be the failures of others. At trial, in its final brief, the Defence emphasised the importance of Macedonian law to establish the role of the minister and the scope of his responsibilities. That is not because the law would permit the ministers to hide from his responsibilities, but because it is that law, the relevant Macedonian law, that enables the minister to carry out his function, and it is that law that sets out the limits of his duties as minister and is relevant to your findings. Functionally, the minister of interior is a political appointee, a manager who heads the ministry. He has no operative competencies but for a limited number of them that have been expressly provided for in the law. As minister of the interior, Mr. Boskoski had no competencies and no duties as regard the investigative activities of the competent organs of the ministry, and his disciplinary competency is narrowly described and his role provided for in the laws and by-laws. The minister does not control, nor is he in charge, of the professional aspects of the work of the ministry. This responsibility lies with the competent operatives at various levels of the ministry, and, ultimately, with the director of the public safety bureau who heads the professional part of the ministry. The minister of interior is not a replacement player, not a substitute for anyone else in the structure of the ministry. He is it not a criminal investigator, he is not the head of a police station, he is not the director of the public safety bureau. And when the Prosecution tries to transfer on to the Ministry of Interior what, in practice, are the obligations and responsibilities of the judiciary over the criminal investigation, Your Honours would be fully entitled to draw inferences from the fact that the Prosecution in this case has called none of the members of the judiciary who had been involved with the Ljuboten investigation. And when asked to draw certain inferences about the minister's role and powers in the disciplinary context, the Chamber would be equally entitled to draw the necessary inferences from the fact that the Prosecution did not call anyone from the disciplinary commission to give evidence. There is another aspect that does not fit within international law, and that is the suggestion that the minister was required to personally involve himself into this matter. International law requires a superior to make a good faith attempt to contribute to the investigative effort. The form that this may take in practice will vary from one case to the other, depending on the circumstances, the legal order in question, and the position of the accused. Focussing for a moment on the requirements of international law, it can be underlined that international law does not require that the superior should carry out any of the investigative work himself or that he should involve himself permanently into the matter. A superior could fulfil his duty to punish by ensuring that the competent investigative bodies are seized of the matter, as was done in the present case. Contrary to the Prosecution allegation, international law does not support the suggestion that the superior would be required to appoint anyone to that task or to set up a new investigative structure if one is already in place. In Ford versus Garcia, for instance, a case from an American US appeal Court that relies heavily on the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the court said the following: "A commander may be relieved of the duty to investigate or to punish wrongdoers if a higher military or civilian authority establishes a mechanism to identify and punish the wrongdoers. In such a situation, the commander must simply do nothing to impede nor frustrate the investigation." For Your Honours' assistance, we have put a list of authorities at the end of the binder. In this particular case, Your Honours, Mr. Boskoski was, therefore, fully entitled to rely upon the structures and procedures, in particular, the judicial organs that are provided for by law and that are competent to carry out criminal investigations. As was made clear in the Defence final trial brief, those judicial organs were properly seized of the matter as early as 12 August 2001 and were competent to carry out the investigation. And where such a course has been fouled, and unless he is alerted to problems that require his involvement, a superior is entitled to under international law to assume that the matter is being properly investigated by the competent organs. Again, Your Honour, I will cite from that same case, Ford versus Garcia. It says this: "Unless the commander has received information suggesting that the investigative or preventive structure is not working properly, he would be entitled to assume that the mechanism put in place is capable of preventing or punishing those crimes." There is one more point that I would wish to make about what a superior is expected to do according to international law as regard the prevention and pursuant of crimes. One way in which international law deals with its own lack of certainty, and perhaps lack of foreseeability, is to leave a great deal of discretion to those who are supposed to implement it or to comply with it. That is true of the law of superior responsibility. As far as superiors are concerned, Your Honour, international criminal law does not provide for a list of measures that a superior would be required to adopt in a particular situation where he learned of a crime. Instead, international law requires that a superior should take measures that are necessary and reasonable in the circumstances. The element of discretionary power that is imbedded into the concept of necessary and reasonable measures is that of the superior not that of the court. In other words, it is not for the court to decide whether it would have adopted the same measures in the circumstances. The court does not express agreement or disagreements with the means adopted; but, rather, fulfil its role of reviewing the legality of the decision of the superior. The Court does not determine whether the measure which the superior has adopted were reasonable in the circumstances; but whether, in the circumstances, they could reasonably have appeared to be so to the superior. An interesting illustration, Your Honour, of that proposition or that principle may be found in the decision of the Supreme Court of Israel which is concerned not directly with the doctrine of superior responsibility but with a court's review pursuant to the Geneva Conventions of Israel's decision to assign to residence Arabs from the West Bank to the Gaza Strip. This is what Supreme Court said on this point: "In exercising judicial review, we do not make ourselves into security experts. We do not replace the military commander's security considerations with our own. We take no position on the way security issues are handled. Our job is to maintain boundaries and to guarantee the existence of conditions that restrict the military's commander's discretion because of the important security aspects in which the commander's decision is grounded. "We do not, however, replace the commander's discretion with our own. We insist upon the legality of the military commander's exercise of discretion and that it falls into the range of reasonableness determined by the relevant legal norms applicable to the issue." It is not, therefore, for the Chamber in hindsight to replace the assessment that a superior might have made of the situation with its own, but to determine whether the course which he pursued in the circumstances could appear to be a reasonable one to him. In the present case, it is clear that the course chosen by Mr. Boskoski should be regarded as adequate in the circumstances, and it certainly was regarded as such by him. A superior is not only entitled to rely upon others to investigate, but he is also entitled to assume that they are acting diligently and competently, and can, therefore, rely upon the information which they provide to him. He is also entitled, Your Honour, to prefer this information to rumours coming from third parties, particularly, where, as in the present case, those rumours are, for the most part, unverified and unreliable. In its final report on the Shatilla and Sabra massacre, for instance, an Israeli Commission of Judicial Inquiry noted, inter alia, that it ought not to be critical of the Israeli prime minister because did he not on his own initiative take any interest in the detail of the operation and did not investigate the reliability of reports of crimes which he had received, despite the fact of very public reports of violence in that refugee camp. The commission composed of members of the Israeli judiciary said this: "The tasks of the prime minister are many and diversion, and he was entitled to rely on the optimistic and calming report of the defence minister that the entire operation was proceeding without any hitches in the most satisfactory manner." In the present case, Mr. Boskoski was, therefore, fully entitled to rely upon the existing personnel structures and procedures as were in place at the time in Macedonian, both within and outside the ministry; and he was also entitled to rely upon the information which he received from the organs in the ministry. His reaction in the circumstances was prompt as he met, the day after the event, with the head of the OSCE. One that same day, he set up a commission of inquiry and appointing the three most senior officers of the ministry to head this commission. His effort was in good faith and consistent all through the relevant time period and beyond. At all stages, he sought to keep himself informed and made various suggestions to the competent organs within the ministry. It has been established beyond a reasonable doubt, Your Honours, at trial that Mr. Boskoski personally took more than 35 different steps to try to elucidate those events and to support the investigative effort. Most of those measures went far beyond his strict legal documents and additional offers of help which he had made were even rejected. It is quite remarkable that the Prosecution would not address any of those and see how they fit, individually or as a whole, in the theory of a cover-up organised or supported by Mr. Boskoski. His actions were supportive of the efforts of the competent state organs, first among those the state and local Prosecutors to whom Mr. Boskoski and the ministry provided all requested assistance, information, and support. His effort was adequate in the circumstances and his conduct was not that of a man who condoned or acquiesced to the crimes, but those of a man who used his position and authority to advance the investigative effort. His actions were also critical to the entire investigative process. It was Mr. Boskoski who put that process in motion when he sets up a commission of inquiry into those events, later providing the information it had collected to the relevant authorities, including the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, and supporting the initiative of Director Mitevski to recommend an exhumation and autopsy to the judicial authorities. His many repeated undertakings to assist the investigative process were all powerful indications of his and the ministry's readiness to assist the judicial process in this matter. The vocal public support of Mr. Boskoski for the investigation was also an important incentive for the competent organs of the ministry to act diligently. Mr. Boskoski also briefed the government, not once but twice about these events, and he fully embraced and supported the idea of international involvement in this case. The Prosecution allegation that Mr. Boskoski took part in a cover-up is nothing but thin air, naked advocacy that is in denial of the evidence, and oblivious to the requirements of the law. No one piece of the evidence could be read as suggesting any interference on the part of Mr. Boskoski with the investigation or any deliberate and knowing criminal abandonment of his duties. That simply is not the evidence. According, even if Mr. Boskoski was recorded as a superior of the perpetrators at the relevant time, the Chamber would have to find that he fulfilled all those duties as would be relevant to his obligation insofar as pertinent to the doctrine of superior responsibility. The Prosecution case would fail for that reason also. Should the Chamber decide or need to push its finding up to that point, or should it find that Mr. Boskoski was derelict in fulfilling his duties, it would next have to determine if any fault as could be attributed to our client would be such to trigger his alleged superior responsibility. The relevant standard in international law is as follows: "The dereliction of duty would have to be such as to amount to a gross violation of his duties. In effect, the breach must be such as to amount to acquiescence or tolerations of the crimes on his part." Again, I refer to the authority that we listed in our binder. The Prosecution has not established that Mr. Boskoski either acquiesced or tolerated the crimes charged in this case and the evidence demonstrates the very opposite. Mere negligence on the part of a superior would not be sufficient to attract superior responsibility. The case of the Prosecution would fail at that part, too. Your Honours, Mr. President, we submit that the evidence that is now on the record would give the Chamber no valid basis on which to enter a finding of guilt. What the evidence tells you is that Mr. Boskoski and the competent organs of the ministry did what they were required to do, as well as what they could, under the circumstances to elucidate these events and to assist the competent judicial organs who were in charge of that process. The case as now presented to you by the Prosecution is built on assumptions, not evidence, and pays no regards to how things really are. The Prosecution case assumed laws and provisions that do not exist. It presupposes duties and obligation that were never borne by the minister, imagine facts and events that never took place, and supposes evidence that simply does not exist. It is just this lack of connection to a concern with the truth, this indifference to how things really work, legally and factually; and the Prosecution's inability to carry its onus to relevant degree of moral certainty, that means that the case must fail. Your Honours, Mr. President, I'm grateful for your patience and for your attention, and I will now give the floor to Ms. Residovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, my colleague Mr. Mettraux, in his arguments, drew attention to the numerous deficiencies in the Prosecutor's final brief. We have observed erroneous references to evidence, erroneous quotations, incomplete references to evidence, and miss interpretation of the evidence. The Defence does not consider that these errors were intentional, but we wish to draw attention to their existence because they may lead to erroneous conclusions about the facts of this case. Your Honours, we are convinced that in reaching your decision, you will rely on the actual evidence in this case, on the witness testimonies in their entirety, and that the errors that have been made will not influence your deliberations. The Defence wishes to point out that the Prosecutor, in his final arguments, both written an oral, failed to respond to important issues raised in these proceedings, which are important to establish the criminal responsibility of the minister. According to the Defence, the Prosecutor failed to respond to issues concerning the position and powers of the minister, his position in the structure and hierarchy of power. He failed to address the role of the minister in criminal proceedings, to evaluate the functioning of disciplinary proceedings, to state his position on the independence of the organs within the ministry, the public security bureau, and administration for security and counter-intelligence, to state his position on effective control of the police stations. This has already been referred to by my colleague Mr. Mettraux. He has not referred to or identified a single the law prescribing or listings the duties and responsibilities of the minister which the Prosecutor claims the minister failed to carry out. He has not referred to a single precedent which might indicate that a superior in the position at the level of the minister would have the duties which the Prosecutor claims that Minister Boskoski failed to carry out. He did not call an expert for the legal system of Macedonia who would explain the role of the minister and the structure of the government in the Republic of Macedonia. He did not offer a single argument to show that Minister Boskoski knew for -- knew of a single problem in ongoing investigation activities before the judicial and other organs. He did not clarify why the investigative activities concerning the events in Ljuboten would be carried out at the level of the minister of the interior of the Republic of Macedonia; that is, at the state level; although, both the law and the practice show that it was the organs of the department of the interior and sectors of the interior that were in charge of that in accordance with their territorial and subject matter jurisdiction. The Prosecutor does not explain how it would be possible to initiate disciplinary proceedings when not a single perpetrator was not known or identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor does not even attempt to clarify the role of the president in connection with the operation, and overlooks the facts which indicate that it was the president who ordered this operation. Your Honours, in our introductory remarks, we have drawn attention to the fact that the Prosecutor did not call witnesses who could have provided relevant evidence, or he failed to call them, for example, the president of the commission formed of the 13th of August; Goran Mitevski, Zivko Petrovski, the under-secretary for the crime investigation, police, the members of the disciplinary commission, and so on; or, he did not put the relevant facts or evidence to the witnesses he did call. Of course, the burden of proof, in any criminal proceedings, including these, is on the Prosecutor. The Defence does not wish to say that it has right to interfere in the manner in which the Prosecutor presented his evidence. However, the Defence is certain that the Prosecutor did not call these witnesses because he was aware that these witnesses could not corroborate his case. Your Honours, in his final brief, the Prosecutor abides by certain statements for the simple reason that he does not understand the manner in which the Macedonian state is organised; what powers and competence are given to the president and the ministers, including the minister of the interior; how criminal investigations are carried out; who the authorised organs and persons are to conduct disciplinary proceedings; as well as other facts which my colleague Mr. Mettraux has drawn attention to in detail. In part 3 of his final -- of their final brief, the Defence analyses in detail the nature of the role of the minister, the legal basis and sources of competency of the minister which stem from three basis: First, the law; secondly, the decisions of the government; and, thirdly, decisions by the president. In paragraphs 333 and 334 of his final brief, the Prosecutor claims that the minister was not bound by strict application of the law, that there was flexibility in interpreting the law, that he failed to compare his role with the role of the president. The president was said to have a wide scope of discretion and flexibility in interpreting the law and applying his powers. The Defence wishes to point out that this is simply not true, and that this allegation by the Prosecutor is not founded in the evidence. The constitution of the Republic of Macedonia, Exhibit P91, draws a clear distinction between the positions of the president and a minister. Article 79 to 86 of the constitution, which are found in tab 10 of the binder, establishes the original competencies of the president which are not limited. However, in Article 95 of the constitution, which is found in tab 11 of the binder, it is established that the state administration consists of the ministries and other organs of administration. And in paragraph 3, it immediately adds that the work of the administration is governed by a law passed by two thirds majority in the parliament. The law on the organisation and work of the organs of state administration, Exhibit P92, tab 12 of the binder, and in Article 49, paragraph 1, all this lists the competencies of the minister in supervising the work of the ministry and his authorities vis-a-vis employees. But it is immediately stated that the minister has these competencies only if these are not otherwise prescribed by the law. In Article 55 of the same law, which has been quoted the more than once here by numerous witnesses, the minister has powers to -- to issue numerous official documents if he is authorised to do so by the law. The law on the government and the rules of procedure, these are Exhibit P551 and P552, and these are in tab 13 and 14 of the binder, prescribes and establishes the responsibility of the minister in implementing the decisions of government or cabinet. The labour law, Exhibit P553, and parts of it are to be found in tab 15 of the binder, establishes the powers and authorities of employers, vis-a-vis employees. The collective agreement establishes that the ministry is the employee and is respected by the minister. Therefore, contrary to the Prosecutor's theory of a broad and flexible application of the law, concerning the powers and authorities of the minister, both the constitution and the law draw a clear distinction between the original authorities of the president which are not limited by the law and the competencies of the minister which are prescribed by the law. Numerous exhibits and pieces of evidence in the proceedings clearly indicate that this was not only the de jure but also de facto position of the ministry, and I refer to the testimony of Vesna Dorevska. In parts 2, 4, and 9 of its final brief, the Defence has analysed in detail the evidence of the role of the Ministry of Interior and the minister in criminal investigations. We wish to draw attention to the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic case. In paragraph 142 the Appeals Chamber establishes that both the Trial Chamber and the parties in the proceedings, both sides in the proceedings, linked their arguments and submissions to the nature of the measures taken. The Appeals Chamber drew attention to the fact that the relevant issue is whether a reasonable trier of fact can conclude that Hadzihasanovic took measures to punish the perpetrators which were necessary and reasonable in the circumstances of the case, rather than whether these measures were disciplinary or criminal in nature. In the Hadzihasanovic case, the Appeals Chamber considered the report of the 20th of August, 1993, and found that this report indicated that there were grounds to suspect seriously whether the 307th Brigade submitted to the public prosecutor in Bugonja a criminal report on the event; and although only murder is mentioned in that report, the Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber erred in not taking into consideration that the report of the 20th of August gave rise to reasonable doubt, reasonable grounds to suspect that the 3rd Corps initiated -- whether the 3rd Corps initiated a report against the perpetrators of murder and cruel treatment. Paragraph 146 of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Appeals Chamber further, in paragraph 148, found in view of the evidence that no reasonable trier of fact could establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the 3rd Corps failed to initiate criminal proceedings. Further, the Appeals Chamber found that no reasonable trier of fact could conclude, based on the evidence, that the measures taken to punish the perpetrators were inadequate in the circumstances of the case. Your Honours, if we go back to the evidence in this case, we shall establish that the Prosecutor, as we already stated in our introductory remarks, was knocking on the wrong door in ascribing to the minister duties he did not have and the responsibilities of other organs in conducting the investigation. Apart from what has already been stated in parts 2, 4, and 9 of the final Defence brief, and in connection with the exercise of the duties of the minister and ministry in taking measures, we wish to point out the following, In the light of the said decision of the Appeals Chamber. In carrying out its responsibility, the ministry acted with urgency. Let us draw your attention to the fact that the evidence indicates that as soon as the 12th of August the duty operative centre informed the investigating judge and the investigating prosecutor of the fact that in the village of Ljuboten there were people who had been killed. That's Exhibit 1D6, tab 23.9 [as interpreted] of the binder; Exhibit 1D71; the testimony of witness M-037; of Petre Stojanovski; of Zlatko Jakovksi and other evidence. On the 14th of August, after new information that in the village there was still bodies of those who had been killed, again, the investigating judge and the prosecutor were informed, with a view to their conducting an on-site investigation. For example, Exhibit 1D6 in tab 23F of your binder as well as the evidence already cited. On two occasions, on the same day, in accordance with the orders issued by the investigating judge, the sector of interior affairs formed a team of forensic technicians to assist the court in the course of the on-site investigation, and this fact is supported by numerous exhibits and pieces of evidence. Let me mention the testimony of Petre Stojanovski. As soon as this information was obtained, the prosecutors and the investigating judge were immediately informed of persons who had been brought in, and pursuant to a decision issued by the investigating judge they were detained in the police station. For example, Exhibit P54.046, and in the binder, it is found in tab 23I. Also, as soon as information was received of the death of Atulla Qaili on the 14th of August, the competent basic public prosecutor was informed of the fact. This follows from Exhibit P46.16, in tab 23 of the binder; Exhibit P261, in tab 23A of the binder; Exhibit P54.030, in tab 23E of the binder; and Exhibit P46.48. All these exhibits show that the competent judicial organs were informed by the ministry of the death of Atulla Qaili. The investigating organs and the investigating judge, as well as the prosecutor, were immediately informed of the injured persons who were in the town hospital. Let me draw attention to Exhibit P262, in tab 23B. That meeting, where all these persons who had been brought in were discussed, when the judicial organs took responsibility for them, the meeting was attended by the acting basic public prosecutor, Lazar Kantrandziski, the deputy public prosecutor, Jovo Serafimovski, and the decision was issued by Judge Beqir Shahini. In connection with this information concerning the injured persons who were brought in, I wish to draw attention to Exhibit P54.052, in tab 23G of the binder; Exhibit P51.20, in tab 23H of the binder; Exhibit P54.046, in tab 23I of the binder; and then in the transcript, the testimony of Isni Ali, transcript page 3471-3472, in tab 24 of the binder; and Exhibit P54.017, in tab 24A of the binder; and other exhibits which clearly indicate that the Ministry of Interior, as soon as it learned of the facts, informed the competent judicial organs. They informed them of all the relevant facts that they found about the events in Ljuboten and elsewhere. Your Honours, the evidence shows that the organs of the ministry immediately, whether orally or in writing, informed the competent judicial organs of all the facts which might be relevant for grounds to suspect that a crime had been committed and that this was a grounded suspicion. Had the Ministry of Interior and the minister taken only these measures and no others, they would have acted in accordance with their legal authorities and fulfilled their duties, and all duties concerning further criminal proceedings would have passed on to the judicial organs. The evidence concerning this is not contradictory, and such evidence has been presented before this Court. First of all, the Law on Criminal Procedure, P88, which indicates clearly that -- and also the testimonies of all the witnesses heard concerning this issue, Vilma Ruskovska and Petre Stojanovski, they all show that once the competent judicial organ has been informed, the duties of the police cease and all responsibility passes to the prosecutor and the judge. In further proceedings, the police is duty-bound to act on orders issued by the prosecutor and the judge. In addition to the measures in part 9 -- in addition to all of these measures, the Defence, in part 9 of its final brief, has listed other numerous measures which the ministry and the minister undertook either on their own initiative or at the request of the judicial organs in order to throw light on all the facts concerning the events in Ljuboten on the 12th and the 14th, and around Ljuboten. Your Honour, we will mention only some of these additional measures. On the 13th of August, the minister immediately formed a commission which comprised the most responsible officials in the ministry, whose task was to investigate these events. That's Exhibit P73. The information that the ministry obtained was provided to the coordinating body of the government, which includes ministers who were both Macedonians and Albanians, and then the government or cabinet of the Republic of Macedonia was immediately informed, as stated by my colleague Mr. Mettraux. The conclusions of the government were immediately implemented, as can be seen in Exhibits 1D134 and 1D137. The assistance of international organisations and organs was immediately sought to assist the ministry in investigating the case. I wish to draw attention to the testimony of General Galevski and other evidence is listed in the final brief. I refer to the same when I say that the ministry immediately sought assistance in their investigations from the deputy prime minister, who was an Albanian by ethnicity. In the report of the commission formed by Minister Boskoski, attention was drawn to the need for an exhumation in order to learn the causes of deaths and other circumstances relevant for the checking of the suspicion. That's Exhibit P378. A written initiative was submitted to the judicial organs for the undertaking of investigating activities. That is exhumation and a post-mortem. Exhibit 1D33 and P102. The OTP of the international Tribunal was informed of the information. The organs of the OVR and SVR continued searching for facts of significance for illuminating the case as can be seen from the testimony of Blagoje Toskovski, Petre Stojanovski, Igno Stojkov, and others. In the Hadzihasanovic case, the Appeals Chamber drew attention, in paragraph 154 of the judgement, that the superior does not have to conduct the investigation personally, but can delegate this to another competent organ; and referred to the trial and appeal judgements or decisions in the Blaskic case. In paragraph 547 -- 546 to 547 of their final brief, the Defence has fully stated this standpoint. In this specific case, Minister Boskoski never creased to be interested in the events and urging the bodies to completely and truthfully clarify the case and then take responsibility measures if circumstances for this exist. This is indicated by the testimony of Igno Stojkov and Sofija Galeva-Petrovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Your Honours, the bodies of the Ministry of Interior continued pursuing additional information through the competent bodies. I'm referencing in this respect to the testimonies of Petre Stojanovski, Sofija Galeva-Petrovska, Igno Stojanovski; and in indication to their own activities, they also spoke about activities of others within the Ministry of Interior, Katica Jovanovska, and other individuals and bodies. Established were task forces and commissions with the same task. The communication with the public prosecutor went on, and all information were forward to them. I am indicating here, Your Honours, the testimony of General Risto Galevski; transcript 3626, then 3661, and the statements of Igno Stojkov and Sofija Galeva-Petrovska. The ministry promptly offered complete cooperation and reacted to all requests sent by the international Tribunal in terms of forwarding the evidence that the ministry had available. Despite the undisputable facts in the case, the Prosecutor remains that the activity of the minister and the ministry was non-transparent. It is stated, in paragraph 362 of the Prosecutor's final brief, where the Prosecutor assumes the position that this was the antithesis of transparency. Regarding this issue as well, the Defence provided detailed arguments in its final brief, in paragraph 644 to 648; and at this moment, we feel it is important to stress the following: First, the assertions about the Prosecutor about the lack of transparence on the lack of procedure are completely unfounded. The evidence led before this honourable Court show that the Minister Boskoski, already on the 14th of August, 2001, in a public statement expressed the interest that all facts are investigated and he announced that an exhumation would be needed. In the report of the committee established by Minister Boskoski, or rather, about that report, all relative bodies were informed, as I indicated before. He invited all interested international organisations to participate in the further course of the investigation, and the report was submitted to the office of the ICTY in Skopje. He publicly and personally expressed his faith in the work of the justice system bodies, and the cases were within their remit of competence; all cases and also the Ljuboten case. The Prosecutor remains with the position that it was a sham investigation, and asserts this without any foundation for it in the evidence on record. As opposed to this unfounded assertion of the Prosecutor, evidence shows that the committee worked abiding by the law, relying on the bodies of the ministry competent to act in the pre-trial and trial procedure, and in cooperation with other bodies competent to act. I'm referencing here the aforementioned testimony of General Risto Galevski, who stressed that before compiling the report of the committee, they had meetings with the public prosecutor and that such meetings continued after the report was filed. The evidence also shows that the committee -- or commission proceeded urgently and adequately to the circumstances in which it operated. In relation to the conclusion of the Prosecutor in paragraph 343 of his final brief and in relation to the findings of the committee chaired by Mitevski, Exhibit P378, that it was that an occurrence of a presence of a negligible and tolerable degree of individual deviation from the boundaries of prescribed competencies was recorded. In relation to this, we note the Prosecutor failed in the course of the procedure to establish what this notion means: "Negligible and tolerable degree of individual deviation." In the extent to which this notion would be important for the state of mind of Mr. Boskoski, this question should have been put to the witnesses that were able to explain what that notion means, especially General Galevski who was a committee member; but the Prosecutor just read out this part of the information without requesting clarification to this. The Prosecutor also failed to prove that the actions detailed in the document would, in itself, constitute a crime or breach of discipline in relation to which a criminal or disciplinary procedure would be carried out. The Prosecutor also failed to prove that the described actions by their nature would be sufficient to testify about the state of mind of Minister Boskoski. The Appeals Chamber, in the Krnojelac case, clearly established that the information that would pertain in general to crimes are insufficient. It is necessary to prove that the accused was aware, had knowledge of the actions that they are charged with. In this case, the sentence mentioned does not indicate murder, cruel treatment, or wanton destruction, so acts that the accused Ljube Boskoski is charged with. Failing to ask Galevski about it and refraining from questioning Zivko Petrovski and failing to invite Goran Mitevski, the Prosecutor is not able to request from the Court to draw conclusions on the basis of that sentence -- the conclusion that the Prosecutor wishes to draw. In any case, the witness Sofija Galeva explained before this Court that there were only rumours about excessive use of force, and it was impossible to verify those. In paragraph 385 of the final brief, the Prosecutor asserts that Boskoski failed to submit the commission's report to the unit for professional standards or the disciplinary committee. In relation to this, we mention, firstly, from the Exhibit 1D372, and that is response of the Macedonian government to the committee for prevention of torture. In page 1D00-9863, it is clearly visible that the unit for professional standards in 2002 and 2003 was still in the process of establishment, so it was not possible to submit the report to it. The Prosecutor failed to prove whether the report was filed with the disciplinary committee of the sector for internal affairs, Skopje, because the records maintained on disciplinary procedures are kept on the basis of data of known perpetrators against whom a disciplinary procedure could be carried out. To verify this fact, the Prosecutor failed to call any of the members of the disciplinary committee as witnesses. In paragraph 275 of the his final brief, the Prosecutor alleges the suspicion of duty of M-056 as proof of the disciplinary competencies of the minister. In relation to this, the Defence stresses, firstly, suspicion from duty is not a measure within the disciplinary procedure and is not a prescribed sanction. It is not prescribed in the collective agreement, and the Defence argument is in detail in chapter 5 of the Defence final brief. Secondly, a disciplinary procedure could be instituted only against a known violator of working duties. So, even if somebody thought that the suspicion from duty was related to the disciplinary procedure, it is clear, then, that M-056 was a known perpetrator. While in Ljuboten, until this very date, it was not established that there were persons who have committed crimes or violated working discipline. And, finally, the Prosecutor failed to accuse Boskoski that he the duty and needed to suspend from duty persons related to Ljuboten events. Boskoski, on the 18th of June, 2001, established a commission to investigate the allegations about any overstepping of powers on the part of police against the Albanian population; Exhibit 1D113. That commission was chaired by General Zoran Jovanovski. In paragraph 351, the Prosecutor devaluates this effort as well, asserting that just a few days later, Boskoski furiously reacted to the request that those abuses seize. These allegations are not correct since the cited conversation, as indicated in P402, took place several days after 18th of July and not 18th of June, as the Prosecutor asserts, and the furry of Boskoski was related to the violation of cease-fire. Facts, evidence, and arguments presented in the final brief, and in light of the previously quoted verdict of the Appeals Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic case, the Defence believes that no reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Minister Boskoski failed to undertake necessary and reasonable measures to investigate and sanction perpetrators in the circumstances in which the minister acted. In the remaining part of my presentation, I will highlight just several other examples of erroneous and unfounded allegations in the brief of the Prosecutor. There is no proof for the assertion of the Prosecutor, in paragraph 21, that would corroborate that an order was issued (redacted) to fortify the check-points, and there is no evidence indicated that this fortification came about. The witness Petre Stojanovski spoke about it in transcript 9148-9149, 9155, and other page numbers that I indicated in our final brief. The evidence that the Prosecutor indicated in his final brief as allegedly corroborating this position are actually not corroborating this position. Further on, there is no evidence that Ljube Boskoski knew about that order, even if such order existed. Finally, (redacted) (redacted) is in contradiction to the assertion of the Prosecutor that the minister had competencies in relation to the check-points. In paragraphs 13, 233, and 249 of the final brief of the Prosecutor, the Prosecutor completely and erroneously alleges that the violation against civilians and civilian facilities was the established practice, citing to the statement of Petre Stojanovski, in order to demonstrate mens rea of the minister about the actions of the police. In contradiction to this assertion, the witness Stojanovski testifies to the opposite exactly, speaking about the spontaneous reaction of the common folk which the police opposed using all available means in order to save the civilian population. I'm indicating here transcript page 9118, 9119, then 9295 to 9260. This assertion of witness Petrovski is also corroborated by witness Risto Galevski, transcript page 3744, 3745; and Kristo Zdravkovski. In the entirety of th is evidence, as well as other evidence, show that the rumours about the illegal conduct of the police and unlawful conduct of police were not verified nor established. Contrary to the assertions of the Prosecutor, evidence shows that persons indicated in the list shown to witness Popovic became members of the reserve forces as of 16th of August, 2001; that means after the Ljuboten events. This fact that the individuals allegedly who had criminal background whose names were shown to the witness Gjoko Popovski became members of the reserve forces as of 16th of August, 2001 is based on the Exhibit P92 --

In relation to this, the Defence presented its arguments in paragraphs 38 to 42, 115 to 121, and 334 to 341. According to the standpoint of the Defence, the Prosecutor, with regard to the de jure case, moves on to the de facto case in paragraphs 269, 273, and 274 of his final brief.
