utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Tarculovski will present its closing arguments, hoping that we will not be repeating the facts stated in the final brief. The Defence has prepared binders which I will ask the court usher to distribute to you. I will begin my closing arguments with the word of caution to the Trial Chamber, that many parts of the Prosecution's brief are not supported by authorities or references with which the Prosecution would support its claim. Some of the claims of the Prosecution may be misleading to the Trial Chamber, and we urge the Trial Chamber to exercise caution in evaluating the Prosecutor's brief. For example, in paragraph 123 of the written submission of the Prosecution, as well as yesterday, the Prosecution claims that M-052 testified that when Atulla Qaili was allegedly beaten, he was severely beaten when he was brought from the village into the Brace house and that he knew that Mr. Qaili was going to die; however, the sequence of events was not so described by M-052. What the Prosecution is concealing is what M-052 testified in fact, that first, Mr. Qaili was brought on foot by the forces that entered into the village, that nobody from there group beat him, he had light marks on his body, he could walk in a normal fashion, that later he was severely beaten by army reservists who inflicted heavy injuries to Mr. Qaili, and then M 52 stated that he knew that Qaili would die. Furthermore, the claim that Mr. Tarculovski was seen in the Brace house in the company of or in the presence of Minister Boskoski or during the alleged cruel treatment, allegedly based on the evidence of Witness M-037, is not correct. M-037 gave no evidence to that extent. It was a statement read by the Prosecution, one that M-037 did not approve or accept; rather, (redacted) (redacted). In other words, M-037 gave no evidence that would support the claims of the Prosecution on that point. This is in paragraph 69 of the final brief of the Prosecution, and I wish to point to the Court the testimony of M-037 of transcript pages 837 to 876 which is to be found in tab 1 of the binder. In paragraph 143, the Prosecution claims that M-039 testified that the house of Qani Jashari was burned after the deaths of Xhelal Bajrami, Bajram Jashari, and Kadri Jashari. The sequence of events in the testimony of M-039 is different. He firmly claimed during the trial that, first, the house was set on fire and that the persons jumped out from the burning house. What the Prosecution is doing is trying to improve the credibility of witness M-039 because such testimony is not corroborated by witnesses M-088 and M-092, because the Prosecution does not have proof from where and when these houses were burnt. The Prosecution uses part of witnesses' testimony that suits their case while ignoring those segments of the testimony that do not. The Prosecution does not give explanation or reason for this evident cherry-picking and does not succeed in facing up to all the evidence that plainly contradict its case. For example, it uses the testimony of M-037 extensively, to the effect that he positively identified Mr. Tarculovski in the village. However, it regards the part of the testimony to the effect that the Hermeline did not have a machine-gun mounted on it, contrary to the false evidence of, inter alia, Hutsch and several villagers; and that three pieces of weapons and ammunitions were seized after three NLA terrorists fleeing from the Jashari house were neutralized. Further, the Prosecution uses the map of Mr. Ostreni, Exhibit P487, where the places under the control of NLA are marked with yellow, in order to prove which territories of the Republic of Macedonia were under the control of the NLA. However, this map shows that the NLA considered Ljuboten to be under its control because the village of Ljuboten is encompassed in the areas marked with yellow, and the Prosecution still holds to its case that the NLA was not present in Ljuboten. The Prosecution acknowledges that there were at least ten to 15 combatants in the village -- Albanian combatants in the village, who were opposing the advance of the police unit. The question then arises: Who were they, if not the NLA? Unless the Prosecution is ready to consider and address the evidence that does not fit their case, then their submissions have no or little value. Your Honours, the Prosecution is attempting to change some of the theory of its case, in important segments of its case, that all victims were innocent civilians. In the final brief, it is stated that it is possible that they were hors de combat. The indictment does not list, nor does it give adequate information or notice, that any of the alleged victims might have been combatants hors de combat. The Defence had no notice of such allegations, and would be prejudiced if this change in the status of the victim is altered. If someone is hors de combat, that means that prior to that, that someone was a combatant, and, therefore, it is in contradiction to the Prosecution's case and theory that there were no such people in the village. The Prosecution, therefore, has to choose what theory it is pursuing and to be candid about it. In the absence of any indication that during the trial the Prosecution changes its theory about the status of the alleged victims, there would be a need for questioning, for instance, of Professor Markovski when a combatant, in fact, becomes hors de combat. This is why this new theory should be ignored as it does not form a part of the Prosecution case. With regard to the alleged joint criminal enterprise, it should be pointed out there is no case pleaded suggesting that the -- that a JCE lasted or existed after the 12th of August, 2001. The allegations of the Prosecution in this regard do not form part of the Prosecution's case and should be disregarded. In fact, the indictment makes it clear that this stopped on the 12th of August. It should be made clear that the indictment does not plead such a case; that there was no notice in the pre-trial brief about such a case; there's no evidence to support such a case; and the allegations do not pertain to any relevant witness. The Prosecution alleges that the objective of the joint criminal enterprise was the unlawful attack on civilians not justified by military necessity. It is alleged that the plan about these deeds came in existence on the 10th of August or, at latest, when the first crimes were commented on 12th August 2001. Nonetheless, the Prosecution does not rely on any specific evidence, although there are many relevant facts; rather, it claims that the evidence considered in its totality demonstrate the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. Such vague construct is not supported by the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. According to the law, there needs to be a common plan to commit these crimes. It is up to the Prosecution to establish beyond a reasonable doubt which of the deeds of the army, police, or the accused Tarculovski amount to planning of these alleged crimes. Evidence has been brought about several meetings on which the operation was planned. The Prosecution did not point that on any of these meetings there was a plan to kill civilians or to attack civilians. To the contrary, on all meetings of the police and the army, the objective was to neutralize the terrorist group NLA. In fact, it is noticeable that the Prosecution never suggested to their witness, M-052 that he had participated in the JCE. In fact, the Prosecution did not put such a case to him and said that he was not a suspect. Therefore, the Prosecution theory is completely artificial and has no support in the evidence. Your Honours, the Defence submits that, in the village, there were approximately 2.000 civilians and that the police and the army were aware of this fact. However, the operation was not directed towards the civilians or civilian facilities as the Prosecution claims. Defence did not call any witness or evidence against disproportionate use of force. This is not the Prosecution's case, and the Prosecution should not now be allowed to change it because it would gravely prejudice the Defence. The Prosecution should admit its failure to prove its case, rather than to try to change it at the last minute. In any case, the Prosecution failed to establish that the response was disproportionate to the threat posed by the NLA in Ljuboten. With a great deal of caution, the Defence will enter into a discussion to the effect that the attack was proportionate targeting only NLA members that were located in civilian houses in the village and on positions around the village of Ljuboten. The practical application of the principle of distinction requires that those who plan or launch an attack take all feasible precautions to verify that the targets attacked are neither civilian nor civilian facilities, so as to spare civilians as much as possible. The evidence at the trial showed that the army and the police had information that even prior to the events from the 10th to the 12th of August, 2001, the village of Ljuboten was used as a military and logistic base for the purposes of the terrorist group NLA. The army clearly established which houses were being used by the NLA, the terrorist group NLA, which houses from the village of Ljuboten were used by the NLA from the 10th to the 12th of August, 2001. Eye-witnesses from the army stationed on the positions Smok and Bomba identified at least four blocks of houses that were used by the NLA to attack the army and police positions. This information was sent through the chain of command to Major Despodov, who ordered the army to open an attack on the targets. The attack of the army and the police had five targets previously identified by the army in the village, as well as the reinforcement of NLA coming from Matejce and Bel Kamen. The fact that no other part of the village was targeted proves that army and police commanders did not expect excessive civilian casualties. In fact, the targets were carefully selected being ones for which the army was 100 percent sure that it was a place from where fire was coming from by the NLA. Your Honours, when a civilian facilitate is used for military purposes, it loses its status as a civilian facilitate and becomes a legitimate target. In this case, the evidence has shown that the NLA used civilian facilities for military purposes. By deciding to do so, the locations where the NLA was stationed or from where they were shooting loses and lost its protective status. The army and the police targeted only the houses for which there was credible information of having NLA members or civilians taking part in the hostilities, and the army did this taking whatever precautions they could under the given circumstances. There was no carpet shelling and no excessive use of force. What the NLA did was to use protected persons, such as civilians, to render legitimate targets immune from attack, an act prohibited by international humanitarian. The fact that there might have been collateral damage, in particular to property, is a consequence of the failure of the NLA to comply with basic requirements of international humanitarian. The failure of one party to adhere to the rule to separate civilians from combatants does not result in obliterating the obligation on the part of the other side to distinguish at all times between both categories of people. However, the presence of civilians will not render a target immune from attack; although, an attacker must exercise reasonable precautions to minimise incidental or collateral injury to civilian population or damage to civilian objects consistent with the mission and allowable risk of attacking forces. Combatants and other individuals directly engaged in hostilities are considered to be legitimate and military targets and only combatants are allowed to take part in the fighting. Further, the law of war permits the attack of enemy combatants and equipment, and I quote, "at any time, wherever located, whether advancing, retreating, or standing still." This is an quote from the report of the Defence Department to Congress on the conduct of Persian Gulf War, appendix on the role of the Law Of War, of 10th of April, 1992 -- 2002 [as interpreted]. The NLA was a threat to the local population as well as to everyone else around the village and the city of Skopje, which the NLA threatened to attack and shell. The NLA was also a direct threat to the villagers of Ljuboten. It is the NLA that provoked the security forces with shelling from rocket launchers on the 12th, morning, no doubt in an effort to bring them in -- to bring in the Macedonian security forces into the village. The real culprit for what happened in the village are those members of the NLA who thought it was acceptable to murder members of the army and then go and hide among civilians, concealed as civilians. This is a tactic that has proven to work on several occasions, as in Vaksince, Aracinovo, Karpalak, Vejce, and other villages in Shar Planina. The Macedonian security forces took every reasonable precaution to minimise incidental or collateral injury to civilian population or facilities. Due to the enormous precautions of the security forces, no civilian was killed in the cross-fire. No women, no child, no elderly person was hurt in the operation. At this point, we should point out that the principle of the presumption of a person or a target as civilian does not apply in the context of a criminal trial. It is up to the Prosecution to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that, one, the victims were indeed civilians; and, two, that the alleged perpetrators of the crime knew of this and acted despite this knowledge. Your Honours, the operation was legal and constitutional, ordered by the president, the Supreme Commander of the armed forces who had legal authority to issue orders to the army and to the police. Mr. Tarculovski was aware of this fact. Witnesses Keskovski and Despodov testified that the president issued an order and that the forces on the ground acted being aware of this order. Witness Jurisic testified that the troops on the ground were aware of this order as well. Exhibit P304, a report of the events of the army, notes this presidential order. The Prosecution claims that such an order does not exist and that the chain of command was not aware of it. However, the Prosecution uses the testimony of M-052 extensively to substantiate its claims against the accused, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: (redacted) Major Despodov would be in charge of taking measures related to the combat activities. This proves that Sokol Mitrovski was aware of the president's order for undertaking operations in and around Ljuboten, and that Major Despodov was aware of it. The Prosecution ignores this evidence which directly contradicts their case. The president, as Supreme Commander, received daily reports from all intelligence units via sector commanders and the sector for security and intelligence about events of the previous day; and in the case of extraordinary events, the president was able to receive immediate reports from his subordinates. The president received reports from the Ministry of Defence, the intelligence agency, as well as from the services of friendly intelligence services that were active in Macedonia; and on the basis of this information, the president undertook measures and made decisions. The president of Macedonia had available all necessary intelligence that -- that a battalion of the NLA was attempting to enter the village of Ljuboten, to reinforce NLA members in the village, and attack the security forces in Ljubanci and Rastak. This is Exhibit 2D42, to be found in tab 2 of the binder. There was information and intelligence that after the terrorist attack on the 10th of August, 2001, when eight members of the Macedonian army died and eight were injured, members of the NLA withdrew to Ljuboten and took and established defensive position - this is Exhibit P301 which is to be found in tab 4 of the binder, and Exhibit 2D44 in tab 5 of the binder - and was aware of the fact that there were terrorists in the village who were shooting from several positions in the village at the army and that the army responded with their weapons. Exhibit 2D103, to be found in tab 6, and Exhibit 1D85. Every structure of the army and the police had information that Ljuboten was a village full of NLA members and that many villagers were members of the NLA. Even the OSCE had information that NLA has covert presence in the village, and their presence was confirmed there by the OSCE on the 14th of August, 2001. Exhibits 1D23, in tab 7 of the binder; and Exhibit 1D24, in tab 8 of the binder. Reports from other international observers in the area confirm that there were members of the NLA in the village dressed in civilian clothing; Exhibit 1D24. On 11 August 2001, Gzim Ostreni ordered the attack of the villages of Ljubanci and Rastak, which is recorded in the log of the 1st Guardist Brigade on the 11th of August, 2001. This is Exhibit 1D85 and is located in tab 9 of the binder. Moreover, the overall international community was aware that there is NLA presence in the village, that the NLA is using civilian facilities as military installations, that the NLA is using civilians as human shields. Your Honours, after the targets were neutralized and there was no further resistance from the NLA in the village, the attack stopped. The Prosecution did not establish that any of the victims was a civilian at the time of the attack. The victims were either combatants or civilians taking part in the hostilities or levee en masse. There is no excessive damage to any civilian structures, only to houses that were used for military purposes and these were the only ones attacked and damaged. It must be pointed out that the remaining 300 and more houses were left intact and were not touched by the security forces. It must also be further noted that Macedonian houses in Ljuboten also incurred damage. This is Exhibit P412.11 to P412.13. One of the arguments that the Prosecution uses is the claim that Ljuboten was a village without ready or prepared defence positions. However, the Prosecution witness Bolton testified that there were, indeed, villages which NLA presence in them without prepared defence positions. Witnesses, including expert Dr. Markovski, testified that it would be logical [as interpreted] to dig trenches in Ljuboten in view of the fact that the army was located above the village, and these would be easily spotted and neutralized. Your Honours, on page 21 [as interpreted] of the transcript, where it stated "logical," it should, in fact, be "illogical"; line 21 of page 61 of the transcript. As regards mens rea, the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that such an attack must have been conducted with the intent of having the civilian population or individual civilians, or civilian structures as the object of the attack, or with reckless disregard for the consequences. To the contrary, all actors in this operation - the police and the army - acted with the understanding that the attack -- the targets of the attack were NLA members in the village of Ljuboten and the reinforcement that was coming from Matejce. There was no proven intent to commit a crime or to target civilians. Your Honours, allegedly, other members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise were, including but not limited to, Zoran Jovanovski, also known as Bucuk, owner of the Kometa security company; two brothers, Aleksander and Vlado Janevski; Petre Stojanovski, member of the MOI; Ljupco Bliznakovski, member of the MOI; and other unidentified employees of the Kometa security agency who formed part of the police unit allegedly led by Johan Tarculovski. It has not been proven that they took part in this action. Further evidence of misleading final brief of the Prosecution, the Prosecution claims that criminals took part in the group that entered Ljuboten. In paragraph 231, the Prosecution claims that the person called Bucuk was known to be a criminal, and it bases its claim on hearsay testimony of witness M-052, who testified that someone had told him that Bucuk was a criminal and on the testimony of M-056. Nonetheless, M-056 never mentioned Bucuk; and if one reads the footnotes, he -- we can see that he has not stated this. The Prosecution made a huge effort to find evidence of the alleged group that entered the village, that they're criminals, that criminal procedures were led against them. The investigators went to the courts in Macedonia, to the public prosecutor's office of the Republic of Macedonia, and to the Ministry of Interior; however, the only thing they were able to find were some unproven criminal reports from the early 1980s that did not even result in an indictment. Your Honours, the Prosecution uses the testimony of witness M-052 and the fact that he did not want to go to a meeting with the army on 10th August 2001 as further evidence of the criminal purpose. The evidence of M-052 in this regard is yet another attempt by him to limit his responsibility in the events and to avoid the criminal proceeding against him. The Prosecution relies on M-052 to try to establish a joint criminal enterprise; however, M-052 is a completely dishonest witness, who would do anything to avoid potential criminal proceedings, including false testimony against others. Furthermore, the Prosecution never put to M-052 that he was aware of such a criminal plan. We agree with the submissions of the Boskoski Defence that M-052 is an unreliable witness and that his evidence should be disregarded because, in its entirety, it's false, unreliable, and self-serving. Your Honours, the Prosecution claims that the alleged presence of Tarculovski in Ljuboten is proof that he was part of the criminal enterprise; however, there is credible evidence that Mr. Tarculovski was there on the order of the president, with the aim of monitoring the situation and informing him of it. Such practice to send his personal security was used by the president in every major operation undertaken by the security forces. There is no evidence that with his activities, Mr. Tarculovski overstepped the mandate given to him by the president. There is no evidence by any crime witness that Mr. Tarculovski participated in any of the alleged crimes, nor that he in any way assisted, encouraged, or lent moral support to a crime, as the law requires. Even if Mr. Tarculovski had assisted the operation, it does not mean that he participated in the perpetration of any crime or assisted any crime. Such participation of Mr. Tarculovski is not sufficient to establish criminal responsibility. The Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his contribution in the plan should be at least a significant one and he must establish that he participated with the necessary criminal mens rea. No such mens rea has been established. Furthermore, not every type of conduct amounts to a significant enough contribution to a common purpose to establish criminal liability of the accused for the crimes committed. Even if the Trial Chamber were to accept the testimony of witness M-037, that Mr. Tarculovski arrived at the Jashari house after the death of the three NLA terrorists, this does not mean that he was in control of the situation. In fact, M-037 testified that Mr. Tarculovski did not issue orders to anyone. The Prosecution has not challenged the evidence of M-037 in this regard. Even if the Trial Chamber were to adopt the testimony that the weapons were shown to Johan, and that he commented that these were weapons of terrorists, it reflects the state of mind of Mr. Tarculovski who believed that the weapons that were shown to him came from the place from where NLA terrorists were killed. If the Trial Chamber adopts the testimony that Mr. Tarculovski consulted with M-037 about some driving licences, it does not mean that he acted outside the mandate given it him by the president to monitor and to inform him of the situation. It was not alleged that he was present at the location when the alleged crimes were perpetrated but afterwards. Even if he were present, there is no sufficient evidence that Mr. Tarculovski in any way assisted, encouraged, or lent moral support for the alleged crime, as the law requires. This is seen in the Haradinaj trial judgement in paragraph 179. With regard to the theory that Mr. Tarculovski acted with intent to further the criminal purpose, which he allegedly commented to M-037 when saying there is no need for an inspection of the dead bodies because there is a state of war, such theory is flawed. It has not been proven that Mr. Tarculovski gave such comments from the position of authority. There is no evidence that Mr. Tarculovski had the competence or the authority to order such an inspection. There is no evidence that it would have been safe to do so to, to have such an inspection, and what the purpose of such comments would be. Perhaps these were his private comments. In fact, M-037 explicitly testified that Mr. Tarculovski did not issue orders, and that the only reasonable inference is that he could not have issued an order for inspection. The Prosecution does not claim that he had the duty to investigate. It is not established that he such an obligation. In fact, this is evident from his role and position that he did not have such a duty. It has not been established that it would have been possible under the given -- to do so, given the circumstances. Your Honours, the Prosecution is ignoring the obvious threats posed by NLA activity in this area when claiming that on-site inspection was possible while terrorists are shooting from the woods and the houses, and that the NLA and the Kosovo Protection Corps are on an offensive from Kosovo through Radusa to and from Matejce through Ljuboten to attack Skopje. Even the OSCE, when visiting the village on the 14th of August, noted that there were NLA combatants in the village. To carry out an investigation was the duty of other bodies, the prosecutor and an investigative judge. The Prosecution alleges that Mr. Tarculovski was commander of the unit that entered the village, but there is no evidence that he gave an order to any member of the group that entered Ljuboten. There is no evidence that any single one of them was subordinated to him de jure, and this is not even alleged. There is no evidence that any member of the group reported to him. There is no evidence that he would have been able to control any of them, and there is no evidence that he had any contacts with the members of the group during the operation. There is no evidence that he had the power or the authority to issue any orders to members of the army and to the Macedonian security forces that took part in the operation. There is no evidence that anyone sought his advice or approval regarding any aspect of this operation. There is no evidence that Mr. Tarculovski controlled any of the alleged unidentified perpetrators at the time of the alleged crimes. The Prosecution claims that Tarculovski drew his authority from Ljube Boskoski. Still, Mr. Tarculovski never met Mr. Boskoski in or around the village of Ljuboten. He had nothing to do with Mr. Boskoski as regards the operation. He never discussed the operation with him. He never called him during that weekend. The claim of M-052 that Mr. Tarculovski came to (redacted) (redacted) three to five weeks before the events in Ljuboten should be disregarded as uncorroborated and false. It is claimed that this is corroborated by witness M-053; however, M-053 testified that he saw Mr. Tarculovski (redacted) only in August 2001, not three to five weeks before the 10th of August, 2001. M-052 even was caught lying in this regard, (redacted) (redacted), he claimed that Mr. Boskoski called him for the first time regarding Johan on the 11th of August, 2001, on the day when the soldiers were buried. Such tendency to invent things and to fabricate things will be relevant to the Trial Chamber not to put any weight on this testimony. As a further attempt to minimise his role and to avoid potential responsibility, (redacted) (redacted). On the contrary, Major Despodov testified to the fact that Mr. Tarculovski did not ask for any fire support, and the other representatives of the Ministry of Interior informed him that there is an action in the planning and they requested such support. Again, this participation of Mr. Tarculovski is in line with the instruction of the president, to be on the ground and monitor the events. Mr. Keskovski, head of the security of the president, testified that sometimes he, himself, would establish a link between the president and the forces on the ground. The testimony of M-084, that Mr. Tarculovski received 50 bulletproof vests and six radios is uncorroborated. There is no record of this happening; no other witness suggested that this has taken place. Furthermore, even if this had happened, this is no proof of any leadership role. Furthermore, person receiving such materials is generally a lower-rank person who is tasked with receiving this equipment. As a further proof of the alleged criminal intent of the operation, the Prosecution uses the alleged criminal background of unidentified alleged participants in the action. To prove its assertion, the Prosecutor says that, allegedly, two participants in the action had committed crimes and had served prison sentences of two years in total, in 1968 and 1985, respectively. However, even if that had been correct that those persons had committed crimes in 1968 and in 1985, it does not mean that they remain criminals throughout their lives; considering even further that the fact was not proven that they had been in the village at that time and participated in the alleged crimes. The fact that someone has not perpetrated a crime since 1968, proves that the criminal, the penal system works well and that the person has been rehabilitated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski, is that a convenient point, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now, then, and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the joint criminal enterprise took place and who were the members of it. The Prosecution has not proven the common objective of the alleged JCE, it being an unlawful attack on civilians and civilian objects, murder, wanton destruction and cruel treatment in the village of Ljuboten. On the contrary, although the burden of proof is not on the Defence, it has proven that the NLA was present in the village of Ljuboten; NLA had the ambitions to attack the villages of Ljubanci, Rastak, as well as the city of Skopje; the NLA attacked the positions of the Macedonian army and police early in the morning of 12th August, 2001, with mortar fire and infantry weapons; at least five combat positions of the NLA were identified in the village; international observers confirmed the presence of NLA in the village; NLA had successfully targeted army and police positions with snipers and machine-guns and infantry weapons; and reinforcements were coming from Matejce to Ljuboten. The majority of the killed NLA terrorists were wearing black uniforms. There have been NLA terrorists mingling with the local population. There have been NLA members wearing civilian clothes. In one of the alleged victims pockets, ammunition was found. In two of the alleged victims, belts were found on the chest under the clothes. All those involved in the Ljuboten operation acted with the awareness that NLA was present in the village of Ljuboten. NLA had received the order to attack the villages of Ljubanci and Rastak in order to further attack Skopje. The attack against the Macedonian army and police was ordered -- the attack of the Macedonian army and police was ordered by the president of the republic as The Supreme Commander. The NLA members were mingling with the population wearing both civilian clothes and black uniforms. Your Honours, the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Tarculovski participated in any of the alleged crimes or has significantly contributed to the execution of the alleged common purpose. There is no evidence showing that Mr. Tarculovski did anything different, other than to obey the order of the president and to be on the ground and monitor the situation. Such participation of Johan Tarculovski is not criminal by nature and does not aid and abet any criminal plan. It was not shown that he has made a significant contribution to any criminal plan. The Prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Johan Tarculovski shared an intent with the other alleged perpetrators to commit the alleged crimes, or that he was aware that the crimes of murder, wanton destruction, and cruel treatment were natural and foreseeable consequences of the alleged objective of the JCE, and that he knew that such crimes might be perpetrated by the group members, and that he willingly took the risk by joining and continuing to participate in the enterprise. The Prosecution failed to prove that the accused Tarculovski had sufficient knowledge that the additional crimes were a natural and foreseeable consequence. Johan Tarculovski acted with the awareness that the NLA was present in the village, and the action of the Macedonian security forces was based on a presidential order. It has not been established beyond a reasonable doubt that Johan Tarculovski was aware at that time that the three killed individuals were allegedly seen as unarmed civilians by him. On the contrary, weapons and ammunitions such as the Macedonian army and police are not using were found immediately after the killing of these people, and the weapons were allegedly shown to Johan Tarculovski. Two of those individuals were wearing black NLA uniforms, and the third one was wearing civilian clothes; but in his pocket during exhumation, 26 pieces of live ammunition were found which indicates the fact that, although he was wearing civilian clothes, he had been a terrorist. Having seen three killed terrorist, NLA members armed shows Tarculovski state of mind that those were killed terrorists and not civilians. It is alternatively indicated that Johan Tarculovski was aware that the crime of murder, wanton destruction, and cruel treatment were natural and foreseeable consequences of the attaining the objective of the JCE. The Prosecution failed to prove that Johan Tarculovski shared from the very beginning a joint criminal act to unlawfully attack civilians or civilian facilities. He has not demonstrated an awareness o the possibility or probability that such a crimes would take place. The Prosecution asserted yesterday that, with regards to existence of JCE, no agreement between the members was needed. It is corroborated by paragraph 838 from Krajisnik verdict. However, the Appeals Chamber of the Tribunal asserts that an agreement is needed in order to establish criminal responsibility within the JCE, in appeals verdict against Tadic, paragraph 227; and Vasiljevic, paragraph 100. Your Honours, it is was not established that the Prosecutor [as interpreted] has participated in the institutional criminal framework willingly and with the awareness, that he had clearly or indirectly shown his participation in the criminal conduct that the institutional or other framework pertains to. In addition to joining the criminal plan and the intention to commit a crime, he willingly took the risk that he or another participant may perpetrate a crime that the former had foreseen. It is up to the Prosecutor to prove that the accused had knowledge of specific facts or circumstances showing the likelihood that the other participant might commit a planned -- a crime that had not been planned or concerted. It is, again, for the Prosecution to prove whether the general circumstances of implementing the agreed plan were such as to cause it to be extremely probably, therefore foreseeable, that other additional crimes are to be committed. It is clear that if the Prosecution fails to prove this, the indictment should be rejected. It would be contrary to the principles of fair trail to change the burden of proof and to request that the Defence proves that the accused was not aware of the relevant facts or has foreseen the crime and willingly took the risk knowing that a crime is to be committed. The Defence knows that during military action, there is also a risk that something unwanted may happen, as stipulated in Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 41. However, the knowledge of any kind of risk, however low, does not suffice for the imposition of criminal liability for serious violations of the international humanitarian law. The Prosecution case is that the crimes of murder and wanton destruction were foreseeable for Mr. Tarculovski because they were participants in the action who had criminal backgrounds and there was violence against ethnic Albanians following NLA attacks against Macedonian security forces, but this is wrong and this a story for small children. Firstly, it has not been proven that any participant in the action had a criminal background as explained before. Secondly, it is rather inappropriate to assert that there had been violence against ethnic Albanians after NLA attacks. Such assertion is erroneous and it is not corroborated by any evidence. It is true that after the massacres that the NLA committed, there have been incidents by an organised mob where Albanian, but not only Albanian, property was burned in Bitola and Prilep, but no Albanian was injured or murdered. If the Prosecution has accepted the testimony of Blagoja Markovski, it needs to accept as well that he testified to the fact that in Prilep, the army barracks were attacked as well by the mob. Still, neither the police nor the army of took a part in such violence. On the contrary, it was the police who arrested the participants in the riots. The premise of the Prosecutor's theory are erroneously defined. They would make sense if, after the NLA attacks, the police would go to murder and arson in Albanian villages' properties. That was not the case. Your Honours, with regards to the criminal responsibility for the crime of murder, the Trial Chamber must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that any of the victims was a civilian, who had not participated actively in any way in the hostilities. If it has been proven that he been killed by a police member, that they were killed with the intent, that the murderer was aware of the fact that the victim had been an unarmed civilian during the time of the killing, and that Johan Tarculovski, himself, was aware of the protected status of the victims and that they had been killed irrespectively of their status. This should not be taken lightly because this is an element of a crime, and this is a state of or evidence of the criminal nature of the crime itself. It is the duty of the Trial Chamber to bring a conclusion beyond a reasonable doubt that a victim was murdered or exclude the possibility of him having taken part in the hostilities at the time of the death, as seen in Haradinaj trial judgement, paragraph 286. There is clear evidence that the army and the police shot only at the NLA positions that were clearly identified. There is clear evidence that it was the army who killed the NLA terrorists who were fleeing the Jashari house. The Prosecution is misleading the Trial Chamber with the map, Exhibit P595. However, the eye-witness, Grozdanovski, testified that the map is not correct. Even the Prosecution, in its indictment, when find it is suitable for them, asserts that the position Smok of the army of the Republic of Macedonia is 300 metres away from Ljuboten. This is in tab 12. The Jashari house is on the part Ljuboten facing the Smok locality. The Prosecution also disregards the testimony of M-088 and M-092 (redacted), and they testified to the fact that the fire (redacted) was coming from the army position and from behind. Further on, the Prosecution is concealing that, according to the autopsy and ballistic report, Kadri Jashari was hit with one bullet of unknown calibre; and in the rest of the ballistics report, it is impossible to identify all of the bullets found in their bodies. However, a bullet of 7.9 millimetres was recovered in the cemetery near the victims, and it was sent for ballistic expertise; Exhibit 1D222. Further on, it is a testimony of the army that they shot not only with snipers, but also with Kalashnikov. Any of them could have caused the death of the alleged victims. It was even proven that some of the alleged victims were wearing black uniforms, such as the ones that the NLA was using and are in evidence. It is rather strange to see why civilians would wear black jackets and trousers in summer at a temperature of 40 degrees centigrade. It was not established beyond a reasonable doubt that Johan Tarculovski was aware when three killed individual -- that the three killed individuals that he had allegedly seen were unarmed civilians. On the contrary, arms and ammunition that the Macedonian army and police were not using were immediately seized and immediately shown to -- allegedly shown to Johan Tarculovski. The Defence does not oppose the contention that Johan Tarculovski had in good faith a belief that there had been NLA members in the village. That is in paragraph 58. Having allegedly seen three killed NLA terrorists carrying weapons, reflects the state of his mind that those killed were combatants and not civilians, and that the participants in the action were only targeting members of the terrorist group NLA. With regards to the wanton destruction, Your Honours, the destruction of property did not occur on a large-scale, neither was excessive. The attack by the police and the army was targeting the NLA that were in and around the village. It was a textbook example of attack carried out bearing in mind the principle of proportionality. Only houses that were with 100 percent certainty identified as NLA positions were targeted. Also, because of the density of the area where the houses were damaged, it might have occurred that some of the adjacent houses were collateral damage in order to achieve the military objective. Still, it was the NLA 40 decided to use civilian property as a military installation, and they are the real culprits for the damage to the property. As the property was used as military installation, it was not protected pursuant to the laws of an armed conflict. It has not been established beyond a reasonable doubt that the perpetrators acted with the intent to destroy property or with reckless disregard of the probability that property would be destructed [as interpreted] all the participants in the operation, both from the army and the police, acted with the awareness that it was at those very location that the NLA terrorists were located, terrorists who were now resisting the police and the army. The Prosecution argues that it was not possible for the army to have destroyed the houses used by the NLA. Then what happened with at least 60 mortars and cannon grenades which fell exactly at the position where the houses were located. However, in the annex A to the indictment, the Prosecution identifies at least four houses that were damaged by mortar impact. As proven, the Albanian houses had in their yards gasoline and other farming equipment that could have ignited the fire. Even if the police damaged houses with hand-grenades or infantry weapons, it was done in order to dissolve the resistance given by the NLA. It is not strange in urban warfare that hand-grenades are used against houses where it reasonable to believe that the enemy was located. Johan Tarculovski did not share any plan or criminal intent to destruct civilian property on a large-scale in the village of Ljuboten. Mr. Tarculovski was not seen on the locations where allegedly civilian property was destroyed, nor has he assisted or contribute to the execution of the alleged crimes. With regards to mens rea, it is up to the Prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Johan Tarculovski acted with the intention to destroy property in question or in reckless disregard of the likelihood of its destruction. There is no evidence that any of the properties were arsoned intentionally. The confirmed presence of NLA combatants in the civilian houses or their usage of civilian houses and religious facilities as military installations, not only in Ljuboten, but all over Macedonia, would be relevant for any inference sought to be drawn as to the state of mind of Mr. Tarculovski at the time. With regard regards to cruel treatment, Your Honours, there is no proof that Mr. Tarculovski had witnessed any of the alleged cruel treatment, nor that he had been aware of any form of misconduct, nor that he had, himself, contributed to such treatment. There is no evidence that he had been seen at Brace's house or another location. Witness M-037 never testified that Johan Tarculovski had seen that some individuals were mistreated. None of the five witnesses from the Ametovski house recognised Johan Tarculovski as having been present at the time of the alleged cruel treatment. In regards to ordering, Your Honours, Mr. Tarculovski did not have the authority to issue orders to anyone, nor did he do so as it was explained before, nor was he a commander of the unit. There is no evidence of him issuing a single order, let alone an order to commit a crime. The theory of the Prosecution is that, as commander of the unit, he issued orders to subordinates to kill, cruelly treat, and burn houses. Such evidence simply does not exist. The alternative theory of the Prosecution is that he acted with awareness of a substantial likelihood that crimes would be committed. As an example, the Prosecution lists the events in Bitola and Prilep. However, as it was explained already, no Albanian was hurt during these events. The crimes against the property committed in Bitola and Prilep was committed by mobs, not by the police. The Prosecution theory that, whilst leading the police unit in an Albanian village, he should have been aware that crimes can occur is very dangerous and completely illogical. Such dangerous theory would tie the hands of every counter-terrorist unit in the world not to attack terrorist, because previously civilians had burned houses in other parts of the country. The question, then, that arises is: What should have the security forces have done? To sun-bathe while watching the NLA shooting at them or attacking the villages of Ljubanci and Rastak in taking positions to attack Skopje? With regard to planning, Your Honours, with regards to planning, the Prosecution uses the same theory. However, an inference that Johan Tarculovski planned an attack cannot reasonably be drawn from the fact that he was present at one of the meetings between the army and the police. Furthermore, any proven involvement in the planning of a legitimate anti-terrorist operation would not constitute evidence as to his involvement in the planning of the crime. The witness Despodov [as interpreted] testified that he was there only to inform himself whether Major Despodov had received order, and it was clear that other persons from the Ministry of Interior and the army planned the activities related to Ljuboten. There is no evidence to show that Johan Tarculovski did anything other than obey the order of the president, to be present on the ground for the purpose of monitoring the situation. At this meeting, no plans to attack civilians were presented. As for instigation, Your Honours, the Prosecution, again, attempts to misguide by claiming that Mr. Tarculovski was present at the Ametovski house. The testimony of M-037 is different. He claims that he saw Johan Tarculovski on the street, not inside any house, and then saw him trying to get information regarding some driving licences. M-037 did not testify that he saw him beating anyone, nor did he see Mr. Tarculovski being there at the time when the alleged beating occurred, nor that he in any way assisted, encouraged, or lent moral support for the alleged cruel treatment as the law requires, nor given any order to that extent. Should the Prosecution rely on the evidence of M-037, it should rely on its entirety, not only to extract pieces of it out of context. The comment which the Prosecution uses for their claims that Mr. Tarculovski said that the three dead terrorists was directed only at M-037 and it was said that three weapons were shown to Mr. Tarculovski. What was he, in fact, supposed to say? That these are civilians fighting for human rights with Kalashnikov? In any way, this behaviour of Mr. Tarculovski does not step outside the assignment given to him by the president. The theory of the Prosecution that Mr. Tarculovski encouraged the perpetrators by saying that the terrorists were here and instigated them to commit crimes is completely outside the time-frame and the given context. After the death of these three terrorists, no alleged crime occurred in Ljuboten. After the terrorists were neutralized, who were at the last position of the NLA in the village, the group withdrew towards Ljubanci and left the other persons intact. No child, no women, or elderly person was injured. The intention of the group was to kill civilians, that they would go from house to house killing everyone that came in their way, and they are at least 250 houses in Ljuboten. The question, again, rises: Why were only the positions that were identified as NLA positions by the army acted upon? Why did the group on the ground not proceed to other houses and kill another 2.000 civilians or burn 300 houses? Another question that comes to mind is why the security forces could not enter Ljuboten prior to the arrival of the Hermeline. Why could not they have just proceeded as in parade from one part to another part of Ljuboten. Why did witness Sedat Murati, on page 4105, testify that the security forces who were in the village of Ljuboten were frightened that someone might shoot at them? The damage and the casualties are consistent with anti-terrorist operations in urban areas and not with a plan to target civilians or civilian property. Regarding aiding and abetting on the part of Johan Tarculovski, the Prosecution does not pursue the theory that Tarculovski, as the alleged leader of the group, had the obligation to prevent or punish the alleged perpetrators; therefore, we will not be discussing this issue. There is no allegation to that effect in the indictment, nor was this mentioned in the final statement. There is no evidence that Mr. Tarculovski made substantial contribution to any of the crimes charged. Even if it were to shown that he has helped with the preparation of the operation, there is no evidence that he thereby assisted in the committing of the crime. According to the state of mind of Mr. Tarculovski, the operation was legal, and there was no suspicion [as interpreted] that the operation is directed against the NLA. There is no evidence that Mr. Tarculovski was present on the ground of any of the alleged sites or that he encouraged anyone by his presence. There is no evidence that Mr. Tarculovski possessed the relevant mens rea in relation to any of the crimes charged. It has not been established, for example, that Mr. Tarculovski was aware that his acts assist in the perpetration of a specific crime of the principle perpetrator. Lastly, what the Prosecution is doing is wrong. Its method to rely on evidence that suit them, while ignoring evidence that does not, including evidence from its own witnesses, is wrong; and in our view, it is not conducive to the Chamber determining the truth of these events. In theory, that armed forces anywhere in the world should not attack its adversary because crimes against property committed by a civilian mob happened 200 kilometres away in a different context is wrong. The theory that someone is a criminal because in 1968 that person had committed a crime and served a prison sentence of one and a half year and should be treated throughout his whole life as a criminal is wrong. We have full faith in the Trial Chamber that it will evaluate evidence objectively and will establish whether there were really crimes committed in Ljuboten and will then consider about the alleged responsibility of Mr. Tarculovski. The action of the security forces in Ljuboten, in Radusa, were a successful response to the terrorist group, NLA, to attack Skopje from two directions and merge with the two battalions clothed in civilian clothing that were already in Skopje. The action of the security forces was essential to stop the attempt of the terrorist group, NLA, to drag Macedonia into civil war and gave the chance to the legitimate political parties to proceed with the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement. Looking at the entire case which is before you, the only thing that can be concluded is that he did not commit the alleged crimes, nor did he act with awareness that his deeds would assist to the perpetration of these alleged crimes. Johan Tarculovski acted legally, obeying the orders of the president, who was then and remains still perceived as one of the biggest peacemakers on the Balkans, and he should not be punished for it. Acquittal is not only a just decision but the only just decision for this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have concluded the addresses of Defence counsel. Tomorrow, there will be an opportunity for all counsel to respond, and we will adjourn now, to resume at 9.00 a.m. tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of May, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
